issues.legal_issue: Eviction for a tenant’s alterations requires proof that the tenant’s use materially and permanently destroyed or reduced the building’s value or utility.
material_facts: The tenant took an old room for a jewellery business and made changes including bricking up a door and windows, lowering the floor, cutting rafters, erecting pillars and installing a rolling shutter.
The bricked-up openings could be restored, and the floor could be restored without structural impairment; the rolling shutter provided added security for the jewellery business.

The landlord did not plead that the changes materially and permanently destroyed or reduced the building’s value or utility, and the evidence did not establish that effect. The landlord admitted that the room could command higher rent if let again.
issues.conclusion: The landlord failed to prove material and permanent destruction or reduction of the building’s value or utility, so eviction on this ground was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11(4)(ii) of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965 requires both material and permanent destruction or reduction of value or utility; the requirements are cumulative. The effect is assessed from the landlord’s standpoint, and the landlord must prove it. The inquiry depends on the facts, including the building’s nature, the purpose of letting, the contract terms and the nature of the interference. The Court relied on the Kerala decisions in Ahammad Kanna v. Muhammed Haneef, Ayissabeevi v. Aboobaker, Shanmugam v. Rao Saheb, Prabodhini v. Rajammal, Thankappan v. Reji Xavier, Mathew v. Gilbert, Aboobacker v. Nanu and Seethalakshmi Ammal v. Nabeesath Beevi. It also considered Manmohan Das v. Bishun Das, Om Prakash v. Amar Singh, Brijendra Nath v. Harsh Wardhan, Arunachalam v. Thondarperienambi, Vipin Kumar v. Roshan Lal Anand and Waryam Singh v. Baldev Singh, noting that provisions in other enactments may differ and that the governing statutory language controls.

predicates.rent_control_alteration_eviction_case: The proceeding sought eviction of a tenant on the ground that the tenant’s use or alteration of rented premises damaged their value or utility.
predicates.tenant_altered_the_building: The tenant made physical changes to the rented building.
predicates.landlord_proved_material_and_permanent_i: The landlord established that the tenant’s use materially and permanently destroyed or reduced the building’s value or utility.

issues.definition: When an alteration-based rent-control eviction case involves tenant-made changes but the landlord has not proved material and permanent impairment, eviction on that ground is not justified.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant facing eviction for rent arrears may be given time to make the required deposit to avert execution, while the adjustability of a security amount against rent arrears may be left undecided.
material_facts: The tenant had not paid rent from the claimed commencement of the arrears, and he deposited rent during the proceedings.
The landlord held a security amount that was repayable to the tenant when he vacated the premises.

The Court did not finally decide whether that security amount could be adjusted against rent arrears; it gave the tenant time to deposit the arrears and other sums required to avert execution of the arrears-based eviction order.
issues.conclusion: The tenant was given two months to make or complete the deposit required under Section 11(2)(c) to avert execution of the eviction order for arrears; the Court left open whether the security amount could be treated as available for adjustment against rent.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 11(2)(c) of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, a tenant may obtain relief from an arrears-based eviction order by making the required deposit. The Court observed that Section 8 addresses premiums and advances and referred to Issac Ninan v. State of Kerala concerning the validity of provisions on fair rent and advance, and to Modern Hotel v. K. Radhakrishnaiah and K. Narasimha Rao v. T.M. Nasimuddin Ahmed concerning a substantial refundable advance. It expressly declined to decide whether the security held in this case could be adjusted against the arrears and instead allowed time for the required deposit.

predicates.rent_arrears_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding sought eviction of a tenant for unpaid rent.
predicates.rent_remained_unpaid: Rent claimed as arrears remained unpaid when the court considered the eviction order.
predicates.tenant_deposited_rent_during_proceeding: The tenant deposited rent during the eviction proceedings.

issues.definition: In a rent-arrears eviction proceeding where rent remains unpaid and the tenant made a deposit during the case, the tenant may avert the eviction by completing the required deposit within the time granted.
